title: Spiral galaxy Messier 100
caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 100, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
celestial: Messier 100 · constellation Coma Berenices · about 55 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This is Messier 100, a spiral galaxy about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. The picture was made with the FORS1 instrument on Kueyen, one of the telescopes that make up ESO's Very Large Telescope.

It is a composite of five separate images, each taken through a different filter. Four of them, named U, V, R and I, capture broad slices of light from the ultraviolet edge of the spectrum through visible light to the near-infrared. The fifth is a narrow filter that picks out the H-alpha line, the red glow of hydrogen gas, which highlights regions where new stars are being born.

The exposures were short by astronomical standards. The V, R and I images each took 60 seconds, the U image 3 minutes and the hydrogen image 5 minutes. The field is 6.8 by 5.1 arcminutes, with north at the top.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.83 x 5.54 arcminutes) and distance (55 million light years), the frame spans roughly 109,000 × 89,000 light-years. Its light set out about 55 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This composite was made with FORS1 on the VLT's Kueyen telescope, through U, V, R and I filters plus a narrow H-alpha filter for glowing hydrogen. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
filters: 360 nm · Ultraviolet U (Very Large Telescope FORS1)
554 nm · Optical V (Very Large Telescope FORS1)
600 nm · Optical R (Very Large Telescope FORS1)
656 nm · Optical H-alpha (Very Large Telescope FORS1)
768 nm · Infrared I (Very Large Telescope FORS1)
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of the data lie beyond what the eye can see, and the galaxy is far too faint to view this way without a large telescope.
